newsitem.title: UK: Gold experts see small price rise by year end.
newsitem.headline: Gold experts see small price rise by year end.

text.p: Mild price rises were forecast for precious metals by the end of 1997 in a poll of market analysts conducted by Reuters on April 21-23.

But despite a volatile gold price's loss of value so far this year, only two of the ten opinions gathered placed the December 31 bullion price forecast lower than Thursday's $341.15 per ounce morning fix.
The experts were asked to forecast the price of gold, silver, platinum and palladium at the end of the current quarter, third quarter and at year end.

"Gold will be held in check by a mixture of central bank sales and sensitive buyers," said Merrill Lynch metal markets analyst Ted Arnold who forecast a gold price slipping from $343 at the end of June to $325 in the third quarter before recovering to $335 by year end.
The poll showed a mean for year end of $355.50 from a $330.00-$380.00 range, just above the second and third quarter means of $345.80 and $350.00 respectively.
Arnold's view typified the outlook for gold. Analysts were fairly sure the risk of a hefty price fall would be limited to about $330, roughly the average cost of producing the metal.
Australian contributors saw gold and silver prices firming slightly over the year in a fundamentally flat market.
According to Mocatta Base Metals and Macquarie Equities, the gold price would be around $350 and silver at $4.90-$5.00 by year end.

Stephen Briggs, at brokers E.W Balderson in South Africa said, "The gold price is so low that the fundamentals are quite good. The problem is that the market is so nervous at the moment. Any statement coming out of any central bank will see a bearish mood." Briggs saw gold at $370 by year end.
Like most of the analysts, he was more hopeful for silver.
He forecast a $5.60 per ounce price at the end of 1997 compared with $4.72 on Thursday.
The expectations of higher economic growth this year in the major economies will benefit silver with its industrial end uses like photography and electronics.
"If silver moves fast, it can drag other things with it," Briggs said.
Analysts' forecasts for year end silver prices ranged from $4.50 to $5.60 with a mean price of $5.10.

"Silver is the only precious metal which has no special influence on its price and can move on its fundamental and technical background," said Hanspeter Hausherr at Zurich-based Swiss Bank Corporation.
"But there is still a lot of institutional business in the market which will take profits on a price rise," he cautioned while putting silver at $5.25 at year end.

Platinum and palladium attracted mixed views with several analysts like George Topping of Johannesburg's Irish and Menell Rosenburg Inc focusing on the idea that their prices will fall when the supply problems between Russia and Japan are resolved.

Russia is the biggest exporter of palladium and second largest supplier of platinum. Japan is the world's leading consumer of both metals which are used in emission control devices on cars, electronics and jewellery.
Shigeru Ishihara, section chief of precious metals division of Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo said platinum prices are likely to rise toward the end of this year on good platinum demand.

"Global platinum demand from the auto catalyst sector is expected to increase in line with the tightening emission control. In addition to solid platinum demand in Japan from the jewellery and glass sectors, emerging platinum demand in south east Asia countries may help platinum move higher," he said.

But Nobufumi Iimori, manager of commodities investment division of Nihon Unicom Corporation cautioned, "Platinum and palladium, are being dicated by the Russians. By definition if they haven't been selling metal their stockpiles are increasing."
Year end platinum price forcasts ranged from $390 to $402 and palladium from $125 to $160.
